implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library has no Semaphore class, so the dominant realization is concurrent-ruby's Concurrent::Semaphore: acquire(permits = 1) blocks until the requested permits are available, try_acquire(permits, timeout) returns immediately, release(permits = 1) returns permits, and the block form 'semaphore.acquire { ... }' yields and releases afterwards - the release-on-every-exit-path idiom, including when the block raises. Because of the GVL, permits bound I/O-bound interleaving and Fibers/Ractors rather than true parallel execution, but the bound on simultaneous resource users is just as real.
code_sketch:
require 'concurrent'

slots = Concurrent::Semaphore.new(8)

slots.acquire do                 # yields, then releases even on raise
  serve(request)
end
pitfalls: Concurrent::Semaphore#release is unbounded: an extra release raises the count and silently widens the concurrency limit.
The GVL does not make ordering automatic - acquire/release discipline is still required, and a permit held across a blocking call stalls only that thread but still consumes budget.
Ractor isolation forbids sharing ordinary mutable objects across Ractors, so a semaphore used by Ractors must be constructed inside one Ractor or be explicitly shareable.

variants.name: Mutex + ConditionVariable hand-rolled semaphore
variants.idiom_name: Thread::Mutex + Thread::ConditionVariable with a permit counter
variants.implementation_notes: Without the concurrent-ruby dependency, the stdlib primitives are enough to build the same counter: Thread::Mutex guards an integer and Thread::ConditionVariable parks waiters until a permit is returned, with the wait in a loop because ConditionVariable#wait can return spuriously. Ruby also ships Thread::SizedQueue, whose push blocks when the queue is full - the bounded-queue form of the same bound when the protected resource is a work queue rather than a set of slots.
variants.code_sketch:
mutex = Thread::Mutex.new
cond  = Thread::ConditionVariable.new
permits = 8

def acquire(mutex, cond, permits)
  mutex.synchronize do
    cond.wait(mutex) while permits[0].zero?
    permits[0] -= 1
  end
end

def release(mutex, cond, permits)
  mutex.synchronize { permits[0] += 1; cond.signal }
end
pitfalls: ConditionVariable#wait must be called inside the associated mutex and re-checked in a loop; a single if allows spurious wakeups to hand out a permit that does not exist.
Signalling outside the mutex is legal but can lose wakeups if the counter is not updated under the same lock; keep the counter mutation and the signal in one synchronized block.
Thread::SizedQueue#push blocks the producer rather than the consumer, so it bounds queue depth, not concurrent users - do not use it as a drop-in semaphore.
